statement: The platform shall make online learning feel organized.
The platform shall make online learning feel secure.
The platform shall make online learning feel easy to use for everyone involved.
Professors shall be able to teach using the platform.
Professors shall be able to communicate using the platform.
Professors shall be able to share materials using the platform.
Professors shall be able to manage class activities without relying on scattered tools.
Students shall be able to participate using the platform.
Students shall be able to collaborate using the platform.
Students shall be able to access course content reliably from anywhere.
Administrators shall be able to manage users through the platform.
Administrators shall be able to manage courses through the platform.
Administrators shall be able to manage the overall environment through the platform.
The platform shall keep the system secure and under control for administrators.
The system shall require individual user accounts.
The system shall tie login to NJIT credentials or another centrally managed authentication method rather than shared accounts.
Administration shall assign user roles.
Professors, students, and administrators shall each see only the content and functions they are supposed to see based on course enrollment and job function.
Professors shall manage their own classes and materials.
Students shall only access the courses they are enrolled in and participate in those courses.
Administrators shall have broader management access, with auditability and restrictions where appropriate.
Courses should be created and maintained by administrators.
Administrators should provision courses, even if professors help set up the content.
The system should support opening a course for enrollment and activity at the start of a term.
The system should support closing a course when the term ends.
The system should archive a course after it is closed so records and materials remain available as needed while the course is no longer actively used.
The system shall support announcements for class-wide messages.
The system shall support direct messaging for one-on-one communication.
The system shall support group communication for teamwork or class discussions.
The system shall use email notifications for important alerts such as new announcements.
The system shall use email notifications for assignment deadlines.
The system shall use email notifications for messages when users are not actively in the system.
The system shall support live video or audio sessions for lectures or office hours.
Integration with an existing conferencing solution is preferred unless NJIT specifically wants to replace the current conferencing solution.
The conferencing tool to standardize on must be confirmed.
The platform shall allow users to launch a conferencing session from the course page and view the meeting link or schedule in context.
If an external conferencing tool is used, professors shall be able to schedule sessions and students shall be able to join sessions with minimal extra steps.
The platform shall include discussion forums and assignment management.
Discussion forums shall be organized by course and topic.
Professors shall be able to moderate or remove inappropriate forum content.
Students shall be able to post and reply within their enrolled courses.
Professors shall be able to post assignments with deadlines.
Students shall be able to submit assignment files or text responses.
The system shall handle assignment due dates and late submissions.
The system shall notify users about upcoming deadlines or newly posted work.
The system shall include a gradebook.
Professors shall be able to enter and edit grades for their own courses.
Students shall only be able to view their own results.
The system shall allow the professor to configure whether grades appear immediately or only after release.
The grading calculation rules shall support weighted categories.
The system shall not assume NJIT-wide special grading rules such as grade drops or curves as standard beyond basic weighted categories.
The system should allow extra credit and late-work grace periods to be controlled by the professor at the course or assignment level, subject to confirmation.
The system should support normal class sizes without noticeable delay.
The system should remain usable during peak periods such as the start of term, exam periods, and scheduled lecture hours.
For live sessions, low latency should be treated as important.
Instructors shall be able to configure extra credit per assignment or course.
Instructors shall be able to control whether an assignment can be dropped from the final grade.
The platform should support mobile use.
The platform should handle low-connectivity situations as gracefully as possible.
Accessibility should be a priority for the platform.
The system shall retain course materials and submitted assignments for at least the duration of the course.
The system shall preserve version history for edited files.
The system shall enforce file type limits.
The system shall perform malware scanning on submissions.
The system shall allow instructors to tighten submission restrictions for a specific course.
Virtual-EDU shall support students in the learning environment.
Virtual-EDU shall support professors in the learning environment.
Virtual-EDU shall support administrators in the learning environment.
Virtual-EDU shall support communication.
Virtual-EDU shall support collaboration.
Virtual-EDU shall support course activities.
Virtual-EDU shall support user management.
Virtual-EDU shall be a secure online classroom environment for NJIT professors and students to interact much like they would in a physical course setting.
The current needs are spread across multiple tools rather than a single unified system.
The system shall allow people to reliably log in.
The retention period for message records shall depend on NJIT policy and applicable compliance requirements.
The IT and security team shall be involved in the project.
The system shall support integration concerns relevant to the IT and security team.
Academic department staff shall be considered as stakeholders.
The system shall support course setup.
The system shall support user assistance for course-related needs.
The system shall consider accessibility requirements when they exist.
The system shall work for all enrolled users.
Virtual-EDU shall provide NJIT with a secure online learning space that feels close to a real classroom when users cannot be on campus.
The system shall provide professors and students with a reliable way to communicate.
The system shall allow professors and students to share course materials.
The system shall allow professors and students to work together.
The system shall support handling class activities without requiring users to use separate tools.
The system shall give administrators control over access.
The system shall allow professors to run discussions.
The system shall allow professors to give assignments.
The system shall allow professors to communicate with students without a lot of friction.
The system shall support higher student participation in class discussions and course activities.
The system shall reduce missed communications by keeping everything in one system.
The system shall reduce the time professors spend juggling tools.
The system shall support students as a main user group.
The system shall support professors as a main user group.
The system shall support administrators as a main user group.
Students shall be able to submit work.
Professors shall be able to manage their classes.
Professors shall be able to create activities.
Professors shall be able to evaluate student work.
The current work environment is fragmented.
Students shall check for updates.
Students shall download materials.
Students shall ask questions.
Students often have to jump between tools to figure out what is due.
Administrators spend a lot of time enrolling users.
Administrators spend a lot of time fixing access problems.
Administrators spend a lot of time making sure classes and accounts are set up correctly.
The biggest delays usually come from manual coordination and people not knowing where to find the latest information.
The system shall support the start of a term when students are enrolling and classes are being set up.
The system shall support midterms and finals when assignment submission, discussions, and grading activity increase significantly.
During peak academic periods, the system shall remain reliable and easy for professors to update.
During peak academic periods, the system shall provide students with quick access to materials and deadlines.
During peak academic periods, the system shall support administrators in handling account changes and access issues.
The system shall handle grading deadlines and add/drop periods because they create last-minute coordination and support requests.
The system shall make deadlines and files easy to find for students.
The system shall allow professors to manage assignments.
The system shall provide students with timely feedback or notifications.
The system shall control assignment deadlines based on the course setup.
After an assignment deadline, the system shall block submissions unless the professor has enabled late submissions.
The system shall allow late submissions after an assignment deadline only if the professor has enabled that policy.
Administrators shall be able to override account settings when needed.
The system shall provide strong authentication.
The system shall protect data in transit and at rest.
The system shall fit into NJIT’s existing identity and user-management setup.
The system shall work with existing student information or enrollment systems.
Course materials and assignments shall be updated as needed during the term.
After the term, the system shall archive course content and records so they can still be referenced later if needed.
Messages and submissions shall be retained for a defined period for academic or compliance reasons.
Retention rules for messages and submissions shall be tied to university policy rather than left to individual users.
After a term ends, archived course data should remain accessible to the professor.
After a term ends, archived course data should remain accessible to the students who were enrolled.
After a term ends, archived course data should remain accessible to administrators.
Archived course data should be accessible only through controlled access rather than regular class editing.
The system should support keeping records for as long as required.
The system should delete retained records in a secure and auditable way.
If there are legal or compliance holds, the system should preserve those records until the hold is lifted.
The system shall manage users, courses, enrollments, materials, assignments, submissions, grades, and communications as core entities.
The system shall track users' identity details, role, contact information, and account status.
The system shall track courses' course code, title, term, instructor, and enrolled roster.
The system shall track materials' and assignments' titles, descriptions, due dates, ownership, versioning, and visibility.
The system shall track communications' sender, recipients, timestamps, course or group association, and message status.
The system shall track submissions' and grades' timestamps, file references, feedback, and late or resubmission indicators to preserve history.
The system shall organize all course-specific materials, assignments, and communications under the course as the main dependency.
Each assignment shall belong to exactly one course.
Each submission shall belong to exactly one assignment and exactly one student.
Each grade shall belong to one submission.
The professor shall be the grader for grades.
Visibility shall follow enrollment and role.
Students shall only see items tied to their active course access.
The system shall preserve history for materials and assignments when they are updated, so published versions are not overwritten and the state actually published at the time is retained.
The system shall track each user’s unique ID, name, email, role, department or program if relevant, account status, and authentication information tied to NJIT’s login process.
The system shall store each course’s course ID, course code, title, term, section, instructor, enrollment status, and archived state.
The system shall store each material or assignment’s title, description, owner, creation timestamp, update timestamp, visibility, attached files or links, and version history.
The system shall store each assignment’s due date.
The system shall store each communication’s sender, recipients, course or group association, timestamp, content or attachment references, and read or replied-to status.
The system shall record who deleted each item.
The system shall record when each item was deleted.
The system shall record under what authority each deletion occurred.
The audit trail shall cover more than just deletions and data changes.
The system shall record logins and failed login attempts.
The system shall record role or permission changes.
The system shall record access to sensitive course data.
The system shall record file downloads and uploads.
The system shall record posting messages.
The system shall record editing messages.
The system shall record deleting messages.
Virtual-EDU should be highly available during peak academic periods, especially at term start, exam time, and grading deadlines.
Virtual-EDU should have routine backups.
Virtual-EDU should have disaster recovery capability.
Virtual-EDU should have fault tolerance so that a single server or component failure does not take the whole platform down.
Virtual-EDU shall be usable with screen readers.
Virtual-EDU shall support keyboard-only navigation.
Virtual-EDU shall provide good color contrast.
Virtual-EDU shall provide captions or transcripts for any audio or video content.
Virtual-EDU shall support accessible document handling for materials and assignments.
Uploaded files and forms shall not create barriers for students or faculty.
The system shall be checked for accessibility during development.
The platform shall provide a way for users to report accessibility problems directly in the platform.
The system shall support keyboard-only use throughout the main workflows.
The system shall make menus reachable without a mouse.
The system shall make forms reachable without a mouse.
The system shall make assignments reachable without a mouse.
The system shall present content in a clean way.
The system shall use readable text sizes.
The system shall provide proper labels on controls.
The system shall provide alternative text where media is involved.
The system shall provide clear error messages.
The system shall tie error messages to the relevant field.
The system shall allow users to adjust display preferences to improve accessibility.
Accessibility shall be treated as an ongoing operational responsibility rather than only a one-time release check.
The system shall support periodic accessibility audits.
Virtual-EDU shall handle heavy concurrency during peak academic windows without slowing to a crawl or dropping sessions.
Virtual-EDU shall scale up enough to support a large number of simultaneous logins, file uploads, discussion posts, and assignment submissions.
Administrators shall be able to see when Virtual-EDU capacity is getting tight.
The migration should be mostly automated where possible.
Virtual-EDU shall preserve metadata during import.
Virtual-EDU shall preserve permission information during import.
Virtual-EDU shall keep content organized and usable after import.
The conversion process shall preserve as much original structure and context as possible.
The conversion process shall flag anything it cannot map cleanly.
The migration shall prioritize a smooth transition with minimal disruption to active classes.
The migration process shall account for data quality challenges.
The migration process shall account for mismatched formats between old tools and the new platform.
The migration process shall ensure that no sensitive information is exposed during the move.
The migration process shall automate as much of the migration as possible to reduce manual cleanup by staff.
Before going live, the system shall verify that users are matched correctly.
Errors or mismatches shall be queued for review.
Errors or mismatches shall be fixable in a targeted way without restarting the entire migration.
Professors shall be able to enter feedback.
Professors shall be able to review feedback before releasing it.
Professors shall explicitly publish or release feedback when they are ready.
The system shall notify students inside the platform when feedback is released.
The feedback view shall make it obvious which assignment the feedback belongs to.
The feedback view shall indicate whether the grade is final or still provisional.
The feedback view shall present comments and rubric details in a way that is easy for students to understand.
The system shall allow professors to enter grades and comments.
The system shall support releasing feedback to one student at a time.
The system shall support releasing feedback in batches for the whole class.
The system shall avoid triggering the same level of notification for provisional grades as for a confirmed release unless the professor intends it.
The system shall use email and an in-system alert as the main notification channels.
The system shall support reminders.
The system shall prevent provisional grades and sensitive feedback from being exposed too broadly.
The system shall provide instructors with controls to choose what feedback is released, to whom it is released, and when it is released.
The system shall allow a professor to hold grades until the whole class has been reviewed.
The system shall keep comments that include sensitive academic concerns visible only to the student and instructor.
If some students receive feedback early because their work was graded first, the system should support avoiding perceived favoritism by allowing professors to wait and release all feedback together.

When an instructor finishes grading only a subset of submissions early, the instructor may wait to release the comments if the comments include corrections or concerns that should be handled consistently across the whole class.
The system shall define how much control instructors have versus how much notification behavior is standardized across courses.
The default reminder policy should send one initial notification and one reminder after a reasonable delay.
For ordinary items, the reminder window should be about one to two days.
Urgent items should include deadline-related corrections and required academic notices.
A reminder shall be sent when feedback is posted.
Reminders shall be sent only for items marked as important or time-sensitive.
The current process for handling students who ignore important feedback is mostly manual and performed by the instructor.
The current approach becomes difficult to manage when there are many students or when the feedback is time-sensitive.
Automated escalations shall avoid repeatedly alerting students or staff about minor issues in a way that feels too invasive.
The system shall not notify professors about every unread comment.
Virtual-EDU shall use clear defaults for escalation behavior.
Virtual-EDU shall provide limited escalation paths.
Virtual-EDU shall provide instructor controls that let instructors decide what is worth chasing.
The current escalation process is mostly manual.
When a student keeps missing feedback, the professor or TA usually reaches out directly.
In some cases, the professor or TA may mention the missed feedback during office hours or class.
This escalation approach can be effective when the class is small.
The current escalation process does not scale very well.
NJIT shall define a central policy that sets the boundaries for escalation and reminder settings.
Instructors shall be allowed to configure their course settings only within the boundaries established by the central policy.
Professors shall be able to choose reminder timing within an allowed range.
Administrators shall have visibility into course settings to keep the student experience consistent.
Administrators shall be able to override course settings when a course configuration starts causing problems.
For repeated non-response to something truly urgent, the matter may move beyond the professor to a department contact or academic advisor.
Extra escalation should occur only for defined cases.
Defined cases for extra escalation include major assignment risk.
Defined cases for extra escalation include attendance issues.
Defined cases for extra escalation include a pattern that suggests the student may need support rather than just another reminder.
Any policy for extra escalation should be tightly controlled so that those extra escalations are rare and clearly justified.
NJIT shall define a standard policy at the institution level.
The system shall allow instructors to adjust only approved settings such as reminder frequency or who gets copied.
Administrators shall monitor course settings.
The system shall make remote learning feel organized.
The system shall make remote learning feel secure.
The system shall make remote learning feel close to a real classroom experience.
The system shall enable professors and students to communicate easily.
The system shall enable professors and students to share course materials.
The system shall enable professors and students to work together on assignments.
The system shall enable professors and students to take part in class activities without a lot of friction.
The system shall allow an enrolled student to join a course in a natural way.
The system shall allow an enrolled student to follow along online.
The system shall allow an enrolled student to interact online.
The system shall allow an enrolled student to get support from the instructor and classmates online.
The system shall address scattered communication.
The system shall help users find the right materials.
The system shall reduce the need for separate tools that do not work together well.
The system shall support instructors in managing participation.
The system shall support instructors in keeping everyone engaged.
The system shall help students know where to go for updates, assignments, and help.
The system shall enforce security and access control.
The system shall ensure that only enrolled users can access the course environment.
The migration shall bring over the core course content and the active course structure so classes can continue running without restarting from scratch.
The migration shall include course materials such as documents, slides, assignments, announcements, discussion history, and shared resources if those exist.
The migration shall carry over enrolled users and their course memberships.
The migration shall preserve the usual workflows for submitting assignments, posting updates, and accessing the same course spaces.
The system shall clean up duplicate records before loading data.
The system shall flag incomplete records before loading data.
The duplicate cleanup and incomplete-record flagging shall apply especially to user accounts and course enrollments.
The system shall map legacy formats into the new structure in a consistent way.
The system shall review ambiguous records instead of guessing their values.
The system shall ensure access and course membership data are accurate.
The system shall report records that cannot be converted cleanly.
The team shall be able to decide whether unconvertible records are corrected manually or left out.
The first release of Virtual-EDU shall include secure login.
The first release of Virtual-EDU shall include course enrollment and access control.
The first release of Virtual-EDU shall include course pages.
The first release of Virtual-EDU shall include file sharing.
The first release of Virtual-EDU shall include communication between instructors and students.
The first release of Virtual-EDU shall include the ability to post and submit course activities.
Advanced analytics can be deferred to a later phase.
Extra integrations can be deferred to a later phase.
More polished collaboration features can be deferred to a later phase.
Security and user access shall be implemented first.
The course structure and enrollment setup shall be in place before file sharing and class activities can function properly.
Communication may be implemented alongside the course structure and enrollment setup.
Communication shall depend on the user and course context being established first.
The first release shall be considered acceptable if instructors can run a class and students can join.
The first release shall be considered acceptable if students can communicate, access materials, and complete activities without major issues.
The system shall be stable enough that people do not need workarounds for the basic teaching flow.
The system shall be secure enough that people do not need workarounds for the basic teaching flow.
The system shall be usable enough that people do not need workarounds for the basic teaching flow.
The team shall define a clear policy for edge cases such as failed enrollment or access problems.
Security shall take precedence in any situation where there is a risk of unauthorized access.
The system shall remain as simple as possible for routine class tasks so students and instructors can use it without friction.
The system shall allow students and instructors to log in at the start of a typical class.
The system shall support different access handling for guest speakers, late add/drop changes, and special permission cases.
Virtual-EDU shall support more than normal lecture courses.
Virtual-EDU shall support lab sections.
Virtual-EDU shall support discussion-based classes.
Virtual-EDU shall support project-based courses.
Virtual-EDU shall support team-based courses.
Virtual-EDU shall support hybrid classes in which part of the work is online and part is in person.
Normal daily use of Virtual-EDU will be much lower than peak usage.
Virtual-EDU will experience noticeable usage spikes during registration periods.
Virtual-EDU will experience noticeable usage spikes during exam weeks.
Virtual-EDU will experience noticeable usage spikes at the start of term.
Virtual-EDU should remain responsive during busy windows when many students are logging in at the same time.
The system should support cross-listed courses.
The system should support guest instructors.
Cross-listed classes should behave like one shared course space even when students come from different departments.
The system shall clearly separate learning activities from content.
The system shall use terminology that matches the terms NJIT faculty and students already use.
The official term should be "course section" for the enrolled class tied to NJIT records.
When a section assignment change becomes effective, calendar entries and reminders from the old section shall no longer be shown.
If a student is enrolled in multiple sections, the system shall show all applicable calendar entries and reminders.
When a student is enrolled in multiple sections, the system shall make it obvious which section each calendar entry or reminder belongs to so the student can distinguish them.
Already sent reminders should not be erased from the user’s history.
Upcoming reminders should be updated in place if the change is known early enough.
A short grace period may be allowed during the transition if needed for sync delays.
The system shall separate course-wide items from section-specific and subgroup-specific items.
Each post or file shall include a clear label indicating who it applies to.
The system shall surface important participation-related notices in a student's main view when those notices affect the student.
The system shall provide a single priority or important flag for urgent updates.
Messaging should feel near real time during normal use.
File uploads should show progress.
File uploads should be able to handle larger course materials without timing out too easily.
Activity participation should count as recorded as soon as the system confirms the submission or action was received successfully.
Slower loads are acceptable for large files, rich media, or first-time access when the system has to initialize everything.
In normal day-to-day use, the course space should still feel responsive.
If content cannot load all at once, it should appear progressively.
When the network is weak, the system should show partial content and a clear loading state rather than a blank screen.
Anything posted in a section or group shall be visible only to the members of that section or group by default.
Content posted in a section or group shall become visible to the whole course only if the poster intentionally shares it at the course level.
Content posted in a section or group shall become visible to the whole course if the instructor sets it as an announcement that everyone needs to see.
Private messages between individuals shall remain private unless there is an explicit reason to forward or copy them.
Instructors shall be able to post course content in their own sections.
Administrators shall have override access to post, edit, or remove course content when there is a support or policy reason.
Students shall usually be able to create and edit only their own contributions.
If content is shared to a group space, group members may have limited editing rights for collaborative work.
The instructor shall control whether group members are allowed limited editing rights in a group space.
Administrators shall only view user data that they need for their job.
Sensitive user data shall be restricted by role.
Access to sensitive user data shall be logged for audit purposes.
Administrators shall be allowed to intervene in an account or override access for support, security, or policy enforcement purposes.
Changing user roles or deactivating an account should require approval or at least a second review in special cases.
Special-case approval or second review is especially required when changing roles or deactivating an account affects faculty accounts or an active student record.
For user accounts, the system shall automatically merge duplicates only when the match is very strong.
For user accounts, a very strong match includes the same institutional ID or a verified email plus matching name and status.
If there is any conflict in identity details, role, or enrollment history for user accounts, the system shall send the record to manual review instead of guessing.
The system shall exclude course enrollments from automatic merge unless the course code, term, and user identity all line up cleanly.
The system shall avoid bad course-enrollment merges because they could place someone in the wrong class or hide a real enrollment.
Course records shall be kept for a period of time after the course ends.
Faculty and administration shall be able to access course records for audits, grade disputes, and accreditation purposes.
The exact retention period for course records must be confirmed with NJIT policy.
One-off access exceptions shall be allowed only in exceptional cases.
Before granting a one-off access exception, the system shall require documented approval from an appropriate supervisor or system owner.
Before granting a one-off access exception, the system shall require a time limit.
Before granting a one-off access exception, the system shall require confirmation of exactly which data or function the person can access.
One-off access exceptions shall be fully logged.
Notifications should be sent first to the people who need to respond first.
Initial notifications should keep the message minimal.
If an incident may involve privacy or legal implications, the communication should be reviewed before it is sent to the broader audience.
The log shall include the reason for the access exception.
The log shall include any conditions attached to the access exception.
The log shall note who is allowed to review each log entry.
Some log entry details shall be restricted to security staff or administrators only.
Security staff and authorized system administrators shall be able to review the log entries.
If a log entry includes sensitive exception details or student-specific information, visibility shall be tighter by role.
The most sensitive parts of such log entries shall be limited to the smallest set of approved reviewers.
The system shall apply least-privilege access when determining which log details each role can view.
Administrators shall be able to see the full audit record.
Student-specific data shall be masked unless the viewer is explicitly authorized to see it.
When there is doubt about disclosure, the system shall hide sensitive fields until an approved reviewer needs them.
Exceptions should be read-only in most cases, especially when the access is for troubleshooting, review, or a temporary lookup.
Editing or other actions should be allowed only when the exception was explicitly approved for that purpose.
Examples of exceptions explicitly approved for editing or other actions include a grading correction or an administrative update.
When editing or other actions are allowed under an explicitly approved exception, they should be tightly limited and logged.
The initial notice shall state that there is an incident.
The initial notice shall identify what part of the portal or course access is affected.
The initial notice shall describe who is impacted in general terms.
The initial notice shall state what immediate steps people should take.
The initial notice shall withhold detailed student information.
The initial notice shall withhold technical root-cause speculation.
The initial notice shall withhold any information that has not gone through privacy or legal review.
Later updates shall include withheld details once the situation is confirmed and cleared for release.
The system shall indicate whether any deadlines or class activities are being impacted right away.
The first message shall not include anything that could be misleading before the issue is fully reviewed.
The portal shall provide built-in guidance for first-time users.
The portal shall provide a short walkthrough or contextual tooltips.
The portal shall provide simple guidance for students on joining classes.
The portal does not need to include a full training system inside the portal.
The portal shall retry message delivery automatically for a short period when messaging is slow or temporarily unavailable.
If a message still cannot be delivered, the portal shall queue the message until service is restored.
The portal shall not drop undelivered messages silently.
The portal shall provide the sender with a clear delivery status so the sender knows whether another channel is needed.
The system shall impose limits so that messages do not remain queued indefinitely.
The system shall vary sender notifications based on whether a message is still pending, has expired, or has failed.
NJIT’s IT or LMS support team shall own day-to-day support after release.
The development team shall handle larger bugs during the warranty or transition period.
Professors and students shall have a clear support path for contacting the appropriate support contact when something goes wrong.
Routine account issues should stay with NJIT IT support or LMS support.
Potential product defects should be escalated to the development team.
Issues with privacy implications should involve the appropriate campus office.
If an issue is unclear, support should triage it first and then pass it along quickly rather than send users back and forth.

If an issue involves student records, personal data, accessibility, disciplinary concerns, or anything that could violate policy, NJIT IT or LMS support should not make a judgment and should escalate the issue.
NJIT IT or LMS support may handle the technical side of an issue if it is clearly routine.
If there is any real privacy or compliance risk, the campus office that owns the relevant policy area should take over the issue.
Support should make the initial triage call using a simple checklist.
If there is any doubt, support should escalate the issue rather than guess.
The support process shall trigger immediate handoff when a case involves unauthorized access.
Support can continue troubleshooting when the issue is a login issue with no policy or security concern.
Support can continue troubleshooting when the issue is a navigation issue with no policy or security concern.
Support can continue troubleshooting when the issue is a simple feature issue with no policy or security concern.
Any clear evidence that data was viewed by the wrong person is sufficient for immediate handoff.
If an issue has been reproduced more than once, support should stop normal troubleshooting and escalate it.
The threshold for involving the right office in a sensitive issue should be low.
